units.summary: Those who rebuke wrongdoing faithfully receive blessing.
units.principle: Honest correction serves justice.
units.insight: People can support someone who names a wrong truthfully under pressure.
units.application: Name a wrong accurately in a setting where it can be addressed responsibly.

rel.note: Faithful friendship can likewise be expressed through a candid word.

units.notes: The kiss pictures affection or goodwill. A right answer is straight and honest.
units.summary: An honest answer is a gesture of goodwill.
units.principle: Truthful candor can express love.
units.insight: A direct answer can serve someone better when it is given with care.
units.application: Give one honest answer you have been avoiding and choose a fitting manner for it.

rel.note: Careful plans and steady effort are contrasted with haste.

units.notes: Outside work and field preparation secure a livelihood. House may mean a dwelling or establishing a household.
units.summary: Prepare the work that will support a household before building it.
units.principle: Wise planning puts supporting work before dependent commitments.
units.insight: An ambitious project can be made more workable by ordering its steps.
units.application: Identify and complete one prerequisite before expanding a project or commitment.

rel.note: False testimony and lies likewise bring accountability.

units.notes: Without cause can mean without a sound basis. The question exposes the deceit involved.
units.summary: Do not give groundless or deceptive testimony against a neighbor.
units.principle: Testimony needs both a truthful account and a sound basis.
units.insight: A concern can be raised responsibly by separating evidence from suspicion.
units.application: Check the basis of an accusation before repeating it as fact.

rel.note: The wronged person is likewise told to wait for the LORD instead of repaying evil.

units.notes: Rendering according to work echoes God's judgment in 24:12. The speaker here claims repayment for themselves.
units.summary: Give up the resolve to pay back a wrong in kind.
units.principle: Justice can be pursued without taking personal revenge.
units.insight: Seeking protection or a fair hearing can coexist with refusing retaliation.
units.application: Set aside one retaliatory response and choose a responsible way to address the wrong.

rel.note: The ant tends to future needs while the opportunity is open.

units.notes: Field and vineyard name productive land. Devoid of understanding literally means lacking heart or judgment.
units.summary: The observer notices the field of a person who has neglected its care.
units.principle: Practical judgment shows in attending to what has been entrusted to us.
units.insight: A neglected responsibility can be examined while distinguishing avoidable delay from genuine inability.
units.application: Look honestly at one responsibility within your ability that has gone untended.

rel.note: The lazy person's way is likewise pictured as obstructed by thorns.

units.notes: Thorns and nettles crowd productive ground. The stone wall protected the vineyard.
units.summary: Neglect can let a useful field become overgrown and unprotected.
units.principle: Small omissions can accumulate into large losses of usefulness and protection.
units.insight: A visible sign of neglect can help a person choose where to begin repair.
units.application: Choose one visible sign of neglect and take the first step toward repair.

rel.note: The learner is likewise told to consider an observed example and become wise.

units.notes: Considered it well includes taking the observation to heart.
units.summary: Careful observation can turn another person's neglected field into instruction.
units.principle: Attention turns what we see into practical understanding.
units.insight: An observed failure can be learned from without making it an occasion for contempt.
units.application: Reflect on one example of neglected care and apply its lesson to a responsibility of your own.

rel.note: The earlier sluggard saying uses nearly the same repeated language.

units.notes: A little repeats the language of apparently minor delay. Folded hands picture inactivity.
units.summary: Small postponements can accumulate into habitual neglect.
units.principle: A repeated little choice can shape an entire course.
units.insight: A short first step can interrupt a familiar delay.
units.application: Replace one customary postponement with a brief start on the work.

rel.note: The earlier warning uses the same images of poverty as a prowler and need as an armed man.

units.notes: A prowler arrives unexpectedly. An armed man pictures a need difficult to resist.
units.summary: Habitual neglect can bring want that feels sudden and hard to resist.
units.principle: Repeated neglect can produce consequences that are hard to reverse.
units.insight: People facing need deserve practical care and a fair hearing about what caused it.
units.application: Address one accumulating cost of neglect while a manageable repair is still possible.

rel.note: Both headings credit collections of sayings to Solomon.

units.notes: Copied means transferred into a written collection.
units.summary: Hezekiah's men copied this collection of Solomon's sayings.
units.principle: Faithful transmission is part of how these sayings reached their readers.
units.insight: Careful preservation can serve people generations beyond those who do it.
units.application: Read this heading alongside the heading at 10:1 and note what each tells you about the collection.

rel.note: A convincing first account likewise calls for further examination.

units.notes: Searching out pictures careful inquiry into a matter.
units.summary: God is glorified in concealing a matter, and kings in searching it out.
units.principle: Good inquiry respects both what can be learned and what God has kept hidden.
units.insight: The limits of our understanding can coexist with careful study.
units.application: Examine the context of a difficult saying before drawing a deeper application.

rel.note: The king's heart, hidden from subjects, remains in the LORD's hand.

units.notes: The height of heaven and depth of earth picture what subjects cannot fully probe.
units.summary: A king's heart can be as inaccessible to subjects as the heights and depths of creation.
units.principle: Limited access to another person's thoughts calls for humility.
units.insight: It is possible to assess a public decision while acknowledging uncertainty about motives.
units.application: Distinguish what a leader did from what you infer they intended.

rel.note: The next verse applies the refining image to removing wicked influence from a court.

units.notes: Dross is impurity removed from metal. Jewelry can mean a crafted object or vessel.
units.summary: Removing dross gives the silversmith material fit for useful work.
units.principle: Removing what compromises a material makes good work possible.
units.insight: Careful preparation can determine the quality of what follows.
units.application: Identify one obstacle that should be removed before you try to improve a process.

rel.note: Righteousness likewise establishes a throne.

units.notes: Taking away the wicked recalls removing dross. Throne refers to a king's government.
units.summary: Removing corrupt influence helps establish a throne in righteousness.
units.principle: Righteous government needs freedom from corrupt influence.
units.insight: A leader can protect others by refusing advice that depends on injustice.
units.application: Remove one source of improper influence from a decision you oversee.

rel.note: Haughtiness precedes ruin, while humility precedes honor.

units.notes: Standing among the great pictures claiming a place of honor.
units.summary: Avoid claiming a place of honor for yourself.
units.principle: Humility governs how we enter a setting where honor is at stake.
units.insight: A person can participate fully without demanding the most visible place.
units.application: Take an ordinary place at a gathering and give attention to someone easily overlooked.

rel.note: Humility likewise comes before honor.

units.notes: Come up here is an invitation to a more honored place. Being put lower pictures public disgrace.
units.summary: It is better to be invited higher than to claim honor and be moved down.
units.principle: Honor is better received than grasped.
units.insight: Humility can be practiced even when recognition never follows.
units.application: Let someone else decide what recognition a contribution deserves.

rel.note: A first account can seem right until the other party examines it.

units.notes: The verb for going to court can also describe pressing a quarrel.
units.summary: Think before pressing a dispute that could expose what you have missed.
units.principle: A claim should be examined before it is pressed publicly.
units.insight: Pausing can leave room for a direct conversation or a fair review of the facts.
units.application: Check the other account and the evidence before escalating a dispute.

rel.note: A faithful person keeps a confidence, while a talebearer exposes it.

units.notes: Debating a case means addressing a dispute. A secret may be the neighbor's confidence or a third person's.
units.summary: Address the dispute directly and guard other people's confidences.
units.principle: Disagreement gives no license to betray a confidence.
units.insight: A truthful conversation can stay focused on what needs to be resolved.
units.application: Take a concern to the person involved without bringing unrelated private information into it.

rel.note: A good name is worth choosing over other advantages.

units.notes: An evil report is damaging talk about the person who disclosed the confidence.
units.summary: Betraying a confidence can leave a lasting mark on one's reputation.
units.principle: Private information should be handled with its lasting consequences in view.
units.insight: An apology can start repair while trust is allowed time to recover.
units.application: If you exposed a confidence, acknowledge it and stop its further spread.

rel.note: A word spoken in its season is likewise commended.

units.notes: Fitly conveys suitability to the occasion. Gold fruit in silver settings pictures beauty and value.
units.summary: A fitting word has the beauty and worth of gold set in silver.
units.principle: Wise speech fits its occasion.
units.insight: The same truth may be easier to receive at a better moment.
units.application: Choose the right moment and a fitting way to say something true and useful.

rel.note: Wise people welcome rebuke and grow through instruction.

units.notes: An earring and ornament picture the value of a correction received well.
units.summary: A wise correction received willingly is like a valuable ornament.
units.principle: Correction bears fruit when wisdom meets a willing ear.
units.insight: A correction can be offered and received in a way that preserves dignity.
units.application: Thank someone for a sound rebuke and take the practical step it calls for.

rel.note: The lazy person irritates those who send him, the opposite of a faithful messenger.

units.notes: The cold of snow in harvest pictures refreshment in hot weather.
units.summary: A faithful messenger refreshes those who rely on him.
units.principle: Faithfulness serves the people who depend on an assignment.
units.insight: Relief can come simply from knowing an entrusted task was done accurately.
units.application: Deliver an entrusted message accurately and confirm that it reached the recipient.

rel.note: Many proclaim loyalty, while proven faithfulness is harder to find.

units.notes: Clouds and wind promise rain that never arrives.
units.summary: A promised gift that never comes is like clouds without rain.
units.principle: Generosity is shown by what is actually given.
units.insight: A modest gift honestly offered can help more than an impressive promise left unmet.
units.application: Fulfill a gift you promised or candidly correct the expectation you created.

rel.note: Gentle speech likewise has power to reduce anger.

units.notes: Long forbearance means sustained patience. Breaking a bone is a picture of overcoming stiff resistance.
units.summary: Patience and a gentle tongue can overcome strong resistance.
units.principle: Patient words can have strength without harshness.
units.insight: Someone can speak gently while remaining firm about what is true.
units.application: Raise a difficult issue in a calm voice and allow the hearer time to respond.

rel.note: The later saying likewise warns against eating too much honey.

units.notes: Honey is a good food. Vomiting pictures what happens when appetite exceeds a fitting limit.
units.summary: Enjoy a good thing in a measure you can bear.
units.principle: Good gifts call for self-control in how they are received.
units.insight: A limit can preserve enjoyment rather than spoil it.
units.application: Choose a reasonable limit for one good thing you tend to overdo.

rel.note: The preceding saying shows how too much of a good thing can become harmful.

units.notes: Seldom setting foot in a neighbor's house warns against wearing out a welcome.
units.summary: Give a neighbor enough space to preserve goodwill.
units.principle: Consideration includes respecting another person's limits.
units.insight: People may welcome company and still need time for their own responsibilities.
units.application: Ask when a visit would be welcome and honor the answer.

rel.note: Rash speech is likewise compared to sword thrusts.

units.notes: A club, sword, and sharp arrow picture weapons that cause real injury.
units.summary: False testimony can injure a neighbor like a weapon.
units.principle: Justice treats harmful falsehood as a serious wrong.
units.insight: An inaccurate accusation can be challenged before its effects spread.
units.application: Correct a false accusation you have repeated and tell those who heard it.

rel.note: A faithful messenger gives relief to those who rely on him.

units.notes: A bad tooth and unstable foot fail when pressure is put on them.
units.summary: Depending on an unfaithful person in trouble can make the trouble worse.
units.principle: Dependability matters most when pressure arrives.
units.insight: People can be given responsibilities suited to the trust they have demonstrated.
units.application: Check who can reliably carry a critical responsibility and make a backup plan where needed.

rel.note: A good word can lift a burden when it fits the person and their need.

units.notes: Removing a garment in cold exposes a person to more discomfort. Vinegar on soda pictures a jarring reaction.
units.summary: Forced cheer can hurt someone whose heart is heavy.
units.principle: Wise encouragement attends to the hearer's actual condition.
units.insight: Quiet presence can offer more comfort than urging someone to cheer up.
units.application: Ask a grieving person what would help today and give them room to answer.

rel.note: Leaving revenge with the LORD gives room to respond with kindness.

units.notes: Bread and water name basic needs. The person in need is an enemy.
units.summary: Give food or water to an enemy who needs it.
units.principle: Love for enemies takes practical form in meeting real needs.
units.insight: Kindness can be offered with boundaries that protect people from further harm.
units.application: Where it is safe, meet a concrete need of someone who has treated you badly.

rel.note: The previous verse specifies the kindness that the coals image follows.

units.notes: The coals are debated and likely picture burning shame or remorse that kindness may awaken.
units.summary: Do good to an enemy and leave the outcome and reward with the LORD.
units.principle: Kindness is a response to evil without becoming another form of it.
units.insight: An act of mercy can be offered without demanding remorse or reconciliation.
units.application: Do a concrete good without using it to embarrass the recipient or demand a return.

rel.note: Whispered talk likewise spreads strife and divides friends.

units.notes: A backbiting tongue is secret slander. The wind and rain comparison has a debated direction in translation.
units.summary: Secret slander and angry reactions are closely connected.
units.principle: Quietly delivered harm still has public consequences.
units.insight: A person can refuse to receive slander without joining the anger it provokes.
units.application: Decline a slanderous conversation and address the actual issue directly if needed.

rel.note: The earlier saying makes the same comparison.

units.notes: A housetop corner is exposed and cramped. The NKJV wording nearly repeats 21:9.
units.summary: A cramped place with peace is better than a comfortable home ruled by strife.
units.principle: Household peace is worth more than space or comfort.
units.insight: Both spouses can examine their own contribution to recurring conflict.
units.application: Choose one recurring quarrel and address it calmly in a safe setting.

rel.note: A faithful messenger likewise refreshes those who rely on him.

units.notes: Cold water refreshes a weary person. News from far away could take a long time to arrive.
units.summary: Good news from far away refreshes like cold water.
units.principle: Good news is worth carrying faithfully to those who need it.
units.insight: A timely update can relieve someone who has been waiting in uncertainty.
units.application: Send a truthful, reassuring update to someone waiting to hear from you.

rel.note: Righteous speech is ordinarily a well of life, the opposite of a polluted source.

units.notes: A muddied spring and polluted well picture a source others can no longer rely on.
units.summary: Giving way to wickedness can muddy a source of help others trusted.
units.principle: Integrity supports others who draw on a person's example.
units.insight: Someone who has compromised can take responsibility and begin repair.
units.application: Identify a pressure to compromise and seek support to keep an upright course.

rel.note: The earlier honey saying urges taking only what is needed.

units.notes: The second line is difficult. The NKJV compares excess honey with seeking one's own glory.
units.summary: Too much honey is harmful, and chasing one's own glory is unfitting.
units.principle: Moderation protects good gifts from being turned into demands.
units.insight: A person can enjoy recognition without making it their aim.
units.application: Do one worthwhile task without calling attention to your part in it.

rel.note: Ruling one's spirit is greater than taking a city.

units.notes: A breached city wall leaves the inhabitants exposed. Ruling the spirit means governing one's reactions.
units.summary: Lack of self-control leaves a person exposed like a city without walls.
units.principle: Self-control guards the choices through which trouble can enter.
units.insight: A small, practiced boundary can help before a strong reaction arrives.
units.application: Practice a specific pause before responding to a familiar provocation.

rel.note: “Luxury is not fitting for a fool” uses the same language of what does not fit a fool.
The same image of snow at harvest appears there as a welcome coolness; here weather out of season pictures what is unfitting.
Both sayings teach that giving honor to a fool is unfitting and self-defeating.

units.notes: Every saying in 26:1–12 except 26:2 mentions the fool by name, gathering the book’s scattered sayings about the fool into one concentrated portrait. Snow appears in 25:13 as a welcome coolness at harvest; here snow and rain out of season picture what is unfitting.
units.summary: Honor given to a fool is as out of place, and as damaging, as snow in summer or rain at harvest.
units.principle: Honor belongs with character that fits it; given to someone who persistently rejects wisdom, it extends his influence and does harm.
units.insight: A community shapes its members by what it honors; praise given to folly quietly teaches that folly pays, while honor given to faithful character strengthens what is good.
units.application: Before praising, promoting or giving a platform to someone, consider his character and conduct, not only his visibility or gifts.

rel.note: Read beside 26:2, the lying tongue that crushes its victims keeps the saying about causeless curses from being turned into a promise that malicious words never cause harm.

units.notes: The traditional Hebrew text carries a scribal note on one small word in the last line. The word written in the text means “not,” while the reading noted in the margin is a word that sounds the same but means “to him.” On that marginal reading, some have taken the line to mean that a causeless curse comes back on the one who spoke it. The NKJV, like the KJV, ESV and NASB, follows the written word, “not.”
units.summary: A curse spoken without cause has nowhere to land, so the one who has done no wrong need not live in fear of it.
units.principle: A causeless curse cannot land, because the LORD, not the speaker, governs what comes to pass. This is a single saying about baseless curses; it is not a full doctrine of curses, and it does not promise that innocent people will never be wronged or hurt by what others say or do.
units.insight: A person who has done no wrong does not have to live under the dread of a baseless curse, because what comes to pass rests with the LORD and not with the one who speaks.
units.application: When someone wishes or pronounces harm on you without cause, entrust the matter to the LORD rather than living in fear of those words; if you have in fact done wrong, deal with that honestly instead of claiming this saying’s comfort.

rel.note: Both sayings assign the rod to the back of one who lacks understanding.
“Beatings for the backs of fools” states the same pattern of hard consequences for fools.
Honor does not fit a fool (26:1); the rod does (26:3).

units.summary: A fool who refuses to be guided by wise words ends up driven by painful consequences, as animals are driven by whip and bridle.
units.principle: Those who reject gentler correction commonly learn through painful consequences; the saying describes the adult fool and does not justify harshness, rage or abuse.
units.insight: When someone refuses wise counsel, hard consequences may be the correction that remains; those who see it should respond with sorrow rather than contempt, and never treat the verse as permission for harshness.
units.application: Listen to wise counsel while words are still enough, and when you must correct others, use fitting and lawful means rather than anger.

rel.note: Supports 26:4: it is honorable to stop striving, since any fool can start a quarrel.
Like 26:4, it counsels against speaking to a fool who will despise wise words.
Shows why leaving the fool wise in his own eyes (26:5) is so serious.
Names the danger 26:5 guards against: being wise in one’s own eyes.

units.notes: The phrase “wise in his own eyes” in 26:5 returns in 26:12 and 26:16, linking the unanswered fool, the self-satisfied man and the lazy man; the book has already warned, “Do not be wise in your own eyes” (3:7). The apparent tension between 26:4 and 26:5 was noticed early. The Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 30b) resolves it by applying “answer a fool” to matters of Torah, God’s law, and “do not answer” to ordinary worldly affairs. That is the Talmud’s own way of dividing the cases, but it agrees that each saying fits a different situation.
units.summary: Wisdom discerns whether a fool’s folly should be left unanswered, so that you do not become like him, or answered plainly, so that he does not become wise in his own eyes.
units.principle: No single rule decides every exchange with a fool; wisdom reads the situation and chooses between silence and a clear answer, and the two sayings complement rather than contradict each other.
units.insight: Believers facing foolish or hostile talk are not handed a formula; they are invited to seek discernment, weighing their own spirit, the person and those listening before they speak or keep silent.
units.application: Before replying to a provocative comment or argument, ask whether answering would draw you into the same spirit, or whether a calm, plain answer is needed so that the error does not stand unchallenged for the person or for those listening.

rel.note: The lazy man is vinegar and smoke to those who send him, another picture of the cost of an unfit messenger.
The faithful messenger refreshes those who send him; the fool as messenger harms the one who sends him.

units.summary: Entrusting an important errand to a fool cripples your own purposes and brings harm back on you.
units.principle: Responsibility belongs with people whose character fits it; the one who entrusts it to a fool brings harm on himself, while the fool still answers for his own misconduct.
units.insight: Choosing whom to trust is part of faithful stewardship; weighing character carefully is not suspicion but wisdom, and it protects both the work and the people it serves.
units.application: When you delegate a task that carries your word or interests, choose someone with a record of faithfulness rather than whoever happens to be available.

rel.note: “Excellent speech is not becoming to a fool” likewise says fine words do not suit a fool.
Shares the same second line; there the proverb in a fool’s mouth becomes harmful rather than merely useless.

units.notes: The Hebrew verb in the first line is uncertain. The KJV speaks of legs that are not equal, while the NKJV and ESV picture legs that hang limp or useless. The comparison’s point is the same in each rendering.
units.summary: A proverb in a fool’s mouth is as useless as legs that hang limp, because he repeats wise words without understanding or living them.
units.principle: Knowing wise words is not the same as being wise; wisdom is shown in a life that understands and practices them.
units.insight: Knowing Scripture’s sayings is a gift, but growth is measured by whether the truth a person can quote is shaping how he lives.
units.application: When you quote a proverb or verse, ask first whether you understand when it applies and whether you are practicing it yourself.

rel.note: Both sayings teach that honor does not belong with a fool.
Together the two sayings warn those who appoint and praise others to look at character before handing out honor or responsibility.

units.notes: The KJV margin records an older understanding of the line as putting a precious stone into a heap of stones, which would picture honor wasted on a fool. The NKJV and most modern translations read the picture of a sling.
units.summary: Giving honor to a fool is as self-defeating as tying a stone fast in a sling.
units.principle: Honor accomplishes its purpose only when it rests on character that fits it; given to a fool, it fails and may rebound on the giver.
units.insight: Those who have a voice in others’ recognition carry a quiet responsibility, because misplaced honor can hurt both the community and the one who gave it.
units.application: When you nominate, promote or publicly praise someone, weigh whether his character will make good use of that honor.

rel.note: Shares the same second line; there the proverb in a fool’s mouth is useless, here it is harmful.

units.notes: The NKJV pictures a thorn that goes into the drunkard’s hand, and the ESV a thorn that “goes up” into it, as the KJV also reads. The NLT has “a thorny branch brandished by a drunk.” Each rendering keeps the point that something hurtful is in hands that cannot manage it.
units.summary: Wise words in a fool’s mouth become dangerous, like a thorn in the hand of a drunkard who cannot handle it.
units.principle: True words used without judgment can do real harm; the fault lies not in the words but in the one who misuses them.
units.insight: Truth can be used to wound; Scripture and wise sayings should be handled with humility and care, especially when they are directed at others.
units.application: Before using a verse or proverb to correct someone, make sure it fits the situation, that you are living it yourself, and that your aim is to help rather than to injure.

rel.note: Affirms that the wicked will not go unpunished.
States plainly that God will “render to each man according to his deeds,” the point the NKJV reading of 26:10 makes.
The alternative translation of 26:10, about hiring a fool, fits the theme of 26:6.

units.notes: The Hebrew of 26:10 is notoriously difficult, and translations differ widely. The word “God” is not present in the Hebrew; the KJV marks it as supplied. The first word of the verse can be read as “great” or as “archer,” and the verb that follows can be read either as forming or producing something, or as wounding. The NLT, ESV and NASB therefore speak of an archer and compare him with someone who hires a fool or passers-by. The NKJV follows the line of the KJV and YLT. The alternative reading fits the theme of 26:6, the folly of entrusting work to a fool.
units.summary: In the NKJV reading, the Creator who formed all things gives the fool and the transgressor the wages they have earned.
units.principle: The Creator does not overlook folly and transgression; in His time each receives his due. Because the Hebrew is difficult, this verse should not carry a major teaching by itself.
units.insight: Those troubled by folly and wrongdoing that seem to go unanswered can rest in the wider biblical teaching that God sees and repays in His time, without resting that confidence on this difficult verse alone.
units.application: When teaching this verse, acknowledge the translation difficulty plainly and support its point from clearer sayings that speak of God repaying each person according to his deeds.

rel.note: Even when ground in a mortar, the fool’s foolishness does not depart from him; both sayings picture folly that does not learn.

units.notes: Peter cites the saying as a “true proverb” and joins it with a second saying about a washed sow returning to the mire (2 Peter 2:22). The second saying is not found in Proverbs.
units.summary: Like a dog returning to its vomit, a fool goes back to the folly that has already harmed him.
units.principle: Folly that refuses to learn from its consequences becomes a repeated habit, and returning to a sin already seen for what it is is both foolish and degrading.
units.insight: The pull back toward a familiar sin is real; seeing how degrading that return is can help a believer keep to the way he has already chosen.
units.application: Name a pattern you have already recognized as harmful, and put specific safeguards in place so that you do not drift back into it.

rel.note: The lazy man wiser in his own eyes shows the same self-deception.
The fool left unanswered becomes wise in his own eyes, the condition 26:12 judges so severely.
Uses the same comparison, placing the man hasty in his words below the fool.
Gives the command and remedy: do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD.

units.notes: The same comparison appears in 29:20, where a man hasty in his words is placed below the fool. Both sayings measure a person against the fool to show how serious his condition is.
units.summary: A man wise in his own eyes is in a worse condition than a fool, because he believes he has nothing left to learn.
units.principle: Self-satisfied pride closes a person to counsel and correction, leaving him less hope than a fool; the fear of the LORD is the remedy.
units.insight: Self-examination can begin with the question this verse asks, and humility before God keeps the door to correction open.
units.application: Ask someone you trust where you may be closed to correction, and receive the answer without defending yourself.

rel.note: The lazy man uses almost the same excuse: a lion outside, and danger in the streets.

units.notes: The NKJV’s “a lion” and “A fierce lion” render two different Hebrew words for lion, which adds to the drama of the excuse. The NKJV uses “lazy man” in all four sayings of 26:13–16, while the ESV and NASB use “sluggard”; the NKJV reserves “sluggard” for 6:6 and 6:9.
units.summary: The lazy man invents a dramatic danger as an excuse to avoid work he can and should do.
units.principle: Laziness often hides behind plausible excuses; the saying exposes invented reasons for avoiding work, not genuine danger, illness, disability or need.
units.insight: Honest self-examination can expose excuses that sound responsible but cover reluctance, while real limits and genuine need deserve compassion rather than accusation.
units.application: When you find yourself explaining why a task cannot be done today, test whether the obstacle is real or is covering reluctance, and take the first step you can.

rel.note: The neglected field of the lazy man shows where this pattern leads.
The sluggard’s “little sleep, a little slumber” and its end in poverty describe the same man fastened to his bed.

units.summary: Like a door swinging on its hinges, the lazy man keeps turning in bed but never gets up.
units.principle: Movement is not progress; the lazy man’s habits keep him fastened to inactivity, and that road leads toward want.
units.insight: Restless motion can disguise a refusal to rise to the work at hand; the way out often begins with one simple, honest step.
units.application: Notice where you are circling a task without starting it, and set a specific time to get up and begin.

rel.note: Nearly the same saying: the lazy man buries his hand in the bowl and will not bring it to his mouth.

units.notes: Where the NKJV has “bowl,” the KJV reads “bosom,” picturing a man with his hands tucked into the folds of his garment. Most modern translations, like the NKJV, read a dish or bowl.
units.summary: The lazy man will not finish even the small effort that would feed him.
units.principle: Laziness is a habit of the will that leaves even necessary and beneficial work unfinished; it is different from genuine weakness or illness.
units.insight: Leaving beginnings unfinished can become a settled habit of the heart; it should be named honestly, while those whose weakness is real are treated with compassion.
units.application: Choose one task you have started and left undone, and finish it before beginning something new.

rel.note: The man wise in his own eyes has less hope than a fool; the lazy man shares that self-deception.
The same phrase, “wise in his own eyes,” describes the fool left unanswered.

units.summary: The lazy man thinks himself wiser than a whole council of sensible people, and that self-deception shields him from correction.
units.principle: A person convinced of his own wisdom will not hear sound counsel, so self-deception becomes the strongest protection of a bad habit.
units.insight: When counsel from several sensible people keeps pointing the same way, humility listens instead of multiplying defenses.
units.application: If several trustworthy people have raised the same concern about your work habits, take it seriously instead of answering each of them.

rel.note: It is honorable to stop striving; the passer-by does the opposite by entering strife that is not his.

units.notes: In Hebrew, the words for “passes by” and “meddles” are built on the same three letters and sound alike. The repetition carries the point: the man who was only passing by becomes, in the very next word, the man caught up in someone else’s quarrel. The second word can also suggest becoming worked up or angry, which is why the KJV margin gives “is enraged” as an alternative for “meddleth,” and the YLT speaks of the passer-by making himself angry over strife not his own.
units.summary: Meddling in a quarrel that is not your own is like grabbing a dog by the ears: easy to start, hard to escape, and likely to end in harm.
units.principle: Interfering in others’ quarrels without a rightful place invites harm; the warning is against meddling, not against honest peacemaking.
units.insight: Concern for others is good, but love asks whether one has a rightful place in a conflict and whether one’s involvement will bring peace or more heat.
units.application: Before stepping into someone else’s dispute, in person or online, ask whether it is truly your concern, whether you have been asked, and whether you would come as a peacemaker or as a partisan.

rel.note: “To do evil is like sport to a fool” describes the same attitude that treats wrongdoing as play.

units.notes: In Hebrew the excuse in 26:19 is a question, asking in effect whether one was not just playing, as the KJV, NASB and YLT render it. The NKJV, ESV and NLT turn it into a statement.
units.summary: The man who deceives his neighbor and then claims he was only joking is as dangerous as a madman throwing firebrands and arrows.
units.principle: Harm done by deception is not undone by calling it a joke; the excuse adds a further wrong by dismissing the neighbor’s hurt.
units.insight: Humor can become a hiding place for cruelty or dishonesty; repentance names the harm honestly instead of minimizing it.
units.application: If a “joke” of yours has misled or hurt someone, drop the excuse, admit the harm and make it right.

rel.note: A whisperer separates the best of friends, another picture of talebearing that sustains strife.
There the contentious man keeps adding fuel; here strife dies when the fuel is removed.
Among the things the LORD hates is “one who sows discord among brethren”; 26:20 shows how such discord is kept alive.

units.summary: As a fire dies without wood, strife dies down when no talebearer keeps feeding it.
units.principle: Strife is often kept alive by repeated stories; when that fuel is removed, conflict can die down.
units.insight: Many conflicts can quiet when someone simply refuses to repeat the story; declining to pass on grievances can be a quiet work of peace.
units.application: When a damaging story about someone reaches you, let it stop with you rather than passing it on.

rel.note: “A wrathful man stirs up strife” states the same pattern.
Uses similar language of a contentious woman, showing the warning applies to men and women alike.
There strife dies when fuel is removed; here the contentious man keeps adding it.

units.summary: A contentious man feeds strife the way charcoal and wood keep a fire burning.
units.principle: A habitually quarrelsome person keeps strife alive and starts new quarrels; in any conflict one either starves it or feeds it.
units.insight: Each person can ask whether he habitually adds fuel to conflict, and pray for a spirit that quiets rather than kindles.
units.application: In a tense conversation, notice the remark that would add fuel to the conflict, and leave it unsaid.

rel.note: The NKJV wording of 18:8 is identical to 26:22.
26:20 shows the talebearer supplying the fuel that keeps strife burning; 26:22 explains why that fuel is accepted: hearers find gossip tasty and willingly take it in.

units.notes: The Hebrew word behind “tasty trifles” occurs only here and in 18:8. The KJV reads “as wounds,” following an older understanding of the word as something that burns or rankles. Hebrew lexicons today take it as food swallowed greedily, and most modern translations, like the NKJV, read it as tasty morsels.
units.summary: A talebearer’s words are tempting morsels that sink deep into the listener and are not easily undone.
units.principle: Gossip appeals to the appetite and lodges deep in the listener; responsibility rests on the hearer as well as the teller.
units.insight: Listening to gossip is not neutral; guarding the heart includes declining what will poison one’s view of another person.
units.application: When a conversation turns to damaging talk about someone who is not present, decline to listen further or steer the conversation elsewhere.

rel.note: There dross is removed so silver can become fine; here dross itself is the deceptive coating.
Develops the same theme of hatred hidden behind pleasant speech.

units.notes: The Hebrew word translated “fervent” means burning or glowing, and the KJV, NASB and YLT render it more literally as “burning lips.” The ESV and NLT have “glaze” in place of “silver dross.” They follow a proposal by the scholar H. L. Ginsberg to read the Hebrew letters behind “silver dross” as a single word meaning glaze, based on a word for glaze found in Ugaritic, an ancient language related to Hebrew, with a parallel word in Hittite. The proposal is a scholarly rereading of the letters, not a Hebrew word attested elsewhere in the Bible, and the NKJV keeps the traditional reading. Either way, the picture is a cheap pot with a shiny surface.
units.summary: Warm words covering a wicked heart are like cheap clay pottery coated to shine like silver.
units.principle: Warm speech can mask a wicked heart; outward appearance is not proof of what lies beneath.
units.insight: The LORD looks past polished speech to the heart, so His people should neither be taken in by appearances nor let their own warmth become a mask.
units.application: Weigh people’s words alongside their conduct over time, and ask whether your own warm words match your heart.

rel.note: “Whoever hides hatred has lying lips” states the same truth about concealed hatred.
The image of a silver-coated clay pot introduces the hidden hatred these verses describe.
“The kisses of an enemy are deceitful” likewise warns that warm gestures can hide hostility.

Uses the same Hebrew verb for covering. In 26:26 deceit covers hatred until it is uncovered before the assembly; in 28:13 the one who covers his sins does not prosper, while the one who confesses and forsakes them finds mercy. Both warn against concealment, with different emphases.

The things the LORD hates in 6:16–19, including “A lying tongue” and “A heart that devises wicked plans,” share the language of detestable conduct with 26:25; the “seven abominations” of 26:25 express fullness rather than pointing to this list.

units.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “covered” in 26:26 is the ordinary word for covering or concealing, the same verb used in 28:13, “He who covers his sins will not prosper.” In 26:26 it is answered by a verb meaning to uncover, translated “revealed”: what deceit has covered, the assembly will see uncovered.
units.summary: Kind words that disguise hatred should not be trusted, and the hidden wickedness behind them remains accountable before God, who sees the heart, even if it is not exposed quickly or within this life.
units.principle: Kind words do not prove goodwill when conduct reveals hidden hatred; concealment is temporary before God, though exposure is not promised to come quickly or within this life.
units.insight: Discernment and love are not opposites: a believer may wish someone well while declining to trust charm that contradicts conduct, and may rest in God’s knowledge of what is hidden without demanding quick exposure.
units.application: When someone’s pleasant words consistently conflict with his actions, let the actions guide how far you trust him, and leave the exposure of hidden motives to God rather than to a campaign of your own.

rel.note: Those who lie in wait for others “lie in wait for their own blood,” the same recoil of planned harm.
The one who leads the upright astray “will fall into his own pit.”

units.notes: Ecclesiastes 10:8 uses the same picture: “He who digs a pit will fall into it.” A similar saying appears later in this collection at 28:10, where the one who leads the upright astray “will fall into his own pit.”
units.summary: The harm a person schemes against others tends to come back on him.
units.principle: In God’s moral world, planned harm tends to recoil on its planner, though the recoil is not guaranteed to be visible or immediate.
units.insight: Those wronged by schemers can entrust justice to the moral order God has built, and everyone is warned that plotting harm is self-destructive.
units.application: Refuse to set traps for anyone, whether through manipulation, sabotage or schemes, remembering that such plans tend to turn against the one who makes them.

rel.note: Traces the same hatred hidden behind pleasant lips that 26:28 names at its root.
The one who rebukes finds more favor afterward than the one who flatters.
The flatterer spreads a net for his neighbor’s feet; flattery works ruin.

units.summary: Lies that crush and flattery that charms both come from a failure of love and leave ruin behind.
units.principle: Deliberate lies and insincere flattery do not come from love, however gentle they sound; both bring ruin on the people who receive them.
units.insight: Love speaks truth; flattery that sounds gentle can harm as surely as a cruel lie, so honest words are worth both giving and welcoming.
units.application: Replace empty compliments with honest, kind encouragement, and be wary of praise that tells you only what you want to hear.

rel.note: People plan their course, and the LORD directs their steps.

units.notes: Boasting about tomorrow presumes knowledge of what the day will bring.
units.summary: Plan humbly because tomorrow's outcome is unknown.
units.principle: Responsible planning leaves room for God's direction.
units.insight: A changed plan can be received without treating it as a personal failure.
units.application: Review one plan and acknowledge to God what lies beyond your control.

rel.note: Seeking one's own glory is likewise judged unfitting.

units.notes: A stranger here means someone other than yourself. Praise echoes boast in 27:1.
units.summary: Let others praise you instead of praising yourself.
units.principle: Honor can be received without being pursued through self-praise.
units.insight: Someone can describe their work accurately without demanding admiration.
units.application: Describe one contribution plainly and credit others who helped.

rel.note: Habitual anger stirs strife and multiplies wrongdoing.

units.notes: Stone and sand picture heavy loads. Wrath pictures the burden a fool's anger creates.
units.summary: A fool's wrath can be harder to bear than a heavy load.
units.principle: An outburst can lay a burden on others that the angry person overlooks.
units.insight: Someone under another person's anger may need help setting limits.
units.application: Stop one angry response before it becomes someone else's burden.

rel.note: Envy is likewise pictured as inward decay.

units.notes: Cruel wrath and overwhelming anger prepare for the question about jealousy.
units.summary: Jealousy can be harder to withstand than an open outburst of anger.
units.principle: A settled resentment can do harm beyond an immediate outburst.
units.insight: Jealousy can be acknowledged before it controls the treatment of another person.
units.application: Name the jealousy behind a reaction and choose a fair response before acting.

rel.note: The following verse explains why a friend's painful words can be faithful.

units.notes: Open means candid. Concealed love remains unexpressed when it could act.
units.summary: Candid correction can serve a friend better than affection left unexpressed.
units.principle: Love becomes useful when it acts for another person's good.
units.insight: A friend can choose a private, caring way to say something difficult.
units.application: Raise a genuine concern privately and explain why it matters to you.

rel.note: A wise person can value the one who offers a needed rebuke.

units.notes: Wounds picture painful correction. Kisses can give a misleading appearance of affection.
units.summary: A friend's painful honesty can be faithful, while an enemy's affection can deceive.
units.principle: Judge a correction by its truth and purpose as well as how it feels.
units.insight: Correction given in love can be distinguished from harshness or humiliation.
units.application: Consider one difficult word from a trusted friend and act on it if it is sound.

rel.note: The honey saying also shows that appetite and limits affect enjoyment.

units.notes: A honeycomb pictures a prized sweetness. Full and hungry describe contrasting appetites.
units.summary: Fullness can make honey unappealing, while hunger makes even bitter food welcome.
units.principle: Appetite and circumstance affect how a gift is valued.
units.insight: What seems ordinary to one person may be a welcome provision to another.
units.application: Receive one ordinary provision with gratitude and share some with someone who needs it.

rel.note: The learner is likewise told to consider the course their feet will take.

units.notes: A wandering bird is away from its nest. Place suggests the setting where one belongs.
units.summary: Restless wandering can leave a person like a bird away from its nest.
units.principle: Leaving a place has costs worth weighing honestly.
units.insight: A move can be considered carefully in light of relationships, obligations, and safety.
units.application: Before leaving a commitment, identify what the move would protect and what it would leave behind.

rel.note: The same friendship can offer a painful truth when that is what will help.

units.notes: Ointment and perfume give pleasure. Hearty counsel is counsel from the heart.
units.summary: A friend's heartfelt counsel can bring real delight.
units.principle: Faithful friendship includes counsel given from the heart.
units.insight: Advice offered with affection can be easier to hear and remember.
units.application: Ask a friend for counsel on a real concern and thank them for the care behind it.

rel.note: Faithful friends and family likewise show their value in adversity.

units.notes: A father's friend represents a friendship carried across generations. Near and far matter in a crisis.
units.summary: Keep faithful friendships, and value a neighbor who is close enough to help in trouble.
units.principle: Faithful relationships are worth tending before adversity.
units.insight: A nearby person can be a source of practical care alongside family ties.
units.application: Reconnect with a long-standing friend or offer timely help to a neighbor.

rel.note: The father likewise rejoices when the child's heart and speech show wisdom.

units.notes: The father's glad heart answers the child's wisdom. Reproach is a charge or taunt against him.
units.summary: A child's wisdom can gladden a parent and answer reproach through conduct.
units.principle: Wisdom can answer criticism through visible conduct.
units.insight: A younger person can be encouraged to act wisely without carrying responsibility for a parent's reputation.
units.application: Choose an upright response that lets your conduct speak for itself.

rel.note: The earlier saying makes nearly the same contrast.

units.notes: Evil here means danger or trouble. The simple are uncommitted and easily led.
units.summary: The prudent recognize danger and take shelter, while the simple proceed into it.
units.principle: Prudence acts on danger it can foresee.
units.insight: A person can learn to notice warning signs earlier.
units.application: Identify one foreseeable risk and take a practical precaution.

rel.note: The earlier saying gives almost the same counsel about taking a garment as security.

units.notes: Surety means guaranteeing another person's debt. A garment could be held as security.
units.summary: A rash guarantee can put the guarantor's own property at risk.
units.principle: A pledge should be weighed by the risk it transfers.
units.insight: A person can offer direct help within their means without cosigning another person's debt.
units.application: Decline a rash guarantee and consider an affordable way to help directly.

rel.note: A word given at the right time is praised, unlike the ill-timed blessing.

units.notes: The loud blessing comes very early. Its effect is reckoned as a curse.
units.summary: A loud blessing at an unwelcome time can feel like a curse.
units.principle: Timing and manner matter in acts of kindness.
units.insight: Good intentions can be expressed in a form the other person can receive.
units.application: Choose a time and manner of encouragement that respects the person receiving it.

rel.note: The earlier saying likewise compares continual contentions to dripping.

units.notes: Continual dripping pictures the wear of a leak that never stops.
units.summary: Persistent contention wears on a household like continual dripping.
units.principle: Small quarrels can do serious harm when they become continual.
units.insight: Both spouses can examine what they contribute to a recurring conflict.
units.application: Change one recurring response that keeps an argument going.

rel.note: The preceding verse identifies the persistent strife these images describe.

units.notes: The Hebrew is difficult. Wind and grasping oil picture what cannot readily be contained.
units.summary: Persistent strife cannot be held in check by force alone.
units.principle: Pressure alone cannot resolve a quarrel rooted in habitual contention.
units.insight: Where conflict persists, seek safe help and address the conduct sustaining it.
units.application: Step back from an attempt to control another person's response and seek a safe way to address the issue.

rel.note: Close company with wise people likewise fosters wisdom.

units.notes: Sharpening iron pictures improvement through contact. Countenance represents the person being sharpened.
units.summary: Faithful friends sharpen one another through honest engagement.
units.principle: Good companions help each other grow.
units.insight: A challenge can strengthen friendship when it is offered with care and received with humility.
units.application: Ask a friend to challenge one assumption and offer equally careful counsel in return.

rel.note: Skillful work is likewise associated with greater responsibility.

units.notes: Keeping a fig tree means tending it. Waiting on a master means attending faithfully to their interests.
units.summary: Faithful attention tends to bear fruit in work and service.
units.principle: Patient care makes useful outcomes more likely.
units.insight: Good work retains value even when it receives little recognition.
units.application: Tend one recurring responsibility with the care needed for it to bear fruit.

rel.note: The heart likewise deserves close attention because the course of life flows from it.

units.notes: Water gives back a reflection. The compressed Hebrew also allows a reading in which one heart reflects another.
units.summary: The heart reveals a person as water reflects a face.
units.principle: Character is seen in what the heart continually reflects.
units.insight: Honest self-examination can bring hidden desires into view.
units.application: Name one recurring desire and ask what it reveals about your present direction.

rel.note: The grave likewise appears among things that never say enough.

units.notes: Hell and Destruction render Sheol and Abaddon. The eyes picture desire for what one sees.
units.summary: Unchecked desire can be as unsatisfied as the realm of death.
units.principle: Appetite needs limits because satisfying it once may only feed it further.
units.insight: Gratitude can help someone notice goods they already have.
units.application: Name one desire you keep feeding and set a specific limit on its pursuit.

rel.note: The same refining image there introduces the LORD's testing of hearts.

units.notes: A crucible and furnace test metals. Praise can reveal a person's character by the response it brings.
units.summary: Praise tests a person as heat tests precious metal.
units.principle: Success and admiration reveal what a person does with honor.
units.insight: Someone can receive appreciation with thanks and still welcome correction.
units.application: When praised, give thanks and name one responsibility you still need to carry faithfully.

rel.note: A single rebuke reaches a wise person more readily than many blows reach a fool.

units.notes: A mortar and pestle crush grain. The image is deliberately extreme.
units.summary: Pressure alone cannot remove settled folly.
units.principle: Correction cannot substitute for a willing response.
units.insight: A person can change direction by becoming willing to learn rather than waiting for greater pressure.
units.application: Act on a sound correction you have resisted before repeating the same conduct.

rel.note: The righteous person likewise attends to the life of an animal in their care.

units.notes: Knowing the state of flocks means observing their actual condition. The command opens a poem through 27:27.
units.summary: Know the condition of what has been entrusted to your care.
units.principle: Stewardship begins with knowing the actual condition of what one tends.
units.insight: Regular attention can reveal needs before they become costly problems.
units.application: Inspect one resource or responsibility you oversee and note what needs attention.

rel.note: Riches can disappear as quickly as an eagle flies away.

units.notes: Riches are stored resources, and the crown represents position or authority.
units.summary: Riches and rank do not last forever.
units.principle: Present security needs continued stewardship.
units.insight: A person can prepare for change by caring for what can sustain ordinary needs over time.
units.application: Review one plan that relies on wealth or position remaining unchanged.

rel.note: The ant likewise gathers food while the season allows it.

units.notes: Cut hay, new grass, and hillside plants mark the cycle of provision. The sentence continues through 27:27.
units.summary: Timely gathering supports the flock through the cycle of seasons.
units.principle: Stewardship pays attention to seasons and their opportunities.
units.insight: People can organize recurring work around the time when it can best be done.
units.application: Identify one recurring task and schedule it when the necessary conditions are in place.

rel.note: The person who tends a fig tree likewise eats its fruit.

units.notes: Lambs supply wool for clothing. Goats supply trade value that can pay for a field.
units.summary: Attentive care of flocks can yield clothing and resources for land.
units.principle: Care of productive resources can sustain a household over time.
units.insight: A modest resource can be valued for the recurring needs it helps meet.
units.application: Identify one resource that regularly meets a need and maintain it with care.

rel.note: Steady work on one's land is likewise associated with enough bread.

units.notes: Enough stresses sufficiency. The milk sustains the household and the maidservants.
units.summary: Diligent care can provide enough for the household and its workers.
units.principle: Good stewardship aims at sufficiency and shared provision.
units.insight: The needs of everyone who depends on a household's work deserve attention.
units.application: Review who depends on one responsibility you manage and make sure their basic needs are considered.

rel.note: Integrity likewise gives security, while crooked ways invite exposure.

units.notes: Fleeing without pursuit pictures fear without an immediate threat.
units.summary: A clear conscience gives courage, while guilt can breed fear.
units.principle: Uprightness gives a sound basis for courage.
units.insight: Confidence can be quiet and steady.
units.application: Address a wrong you have been hiding so you can face it honestly.

rel.note: The king establishes the land through justice, while bribery brings it down.

units.notes: Many princes suggests turnover or rival claimants. The second line is compressed.
units.summary: Wrongdoing destabilizes rule, while discerning leadership helps sustain order.
units.principle: A community's stability depends in part on the character of its rule.
units.insight: People in authority can strengthen continuity through fair judgment.
units.application: Correct one practice that undermines trust in a responsibility you oversee.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor is an affront to their Maker.

units.notes: Driving rain destroys the crop it might have watered.
units.summary: A poor person who oppresses the poor is like rain that destroys the crop.
units.principle: Every measure of power carries responsibility.
units.insight: Shared hardship can prompt solidarity or become an occasion to misuse power.
units.application: Check whether a rule you administer takes unfair advantage of someone with little leverage.

rel.note: Calling the wicked righteous likewise corrupts moral judgment.

units.notes: Law means God's instruction. Contending means actively resisting.
units.summary: Forsaking God's instruction can lead to praising the wicked, while keeping it leads to resisting them.
units.principle: Obedience shapes what we commend and what we oppose.
units.insight: A person can challenge wrongdoing truthfully without resorting to contempt.
units.application: Withdraw praise for a harmful practice and explain your concern honestly.

rel.note: Wisdom from the LORD enables understanding of justice and equity.

units.notes: Understanding all concerns the justice under discussion.
units.summary: Seeking the LORD gives understanding of justice.
units.principle: Knowing God's ways helps us judge rightly.
units.insight: Prayer and careful listening can belong together when weighing a difficult case.
units.application: Bring one disputed decision before God and hear the people it affects.

rel.note: The poor person of integrity is likewise preferred to the person of crooked speech.

units.notes: Walking describes habitual conduct. Perverse ways are crooked dealings.
units.summary: Integrity with little is better than crookedness with riches.
units.principle: Wealth cannot compensate for dishonesty.
units.insight: A person of modest means can be honored for upright conduct.
units.application: Decline a profitable shortcut that would compromise your integrity.

rel.note: The teacher likewise warns against close company centered on excess.

units.notes: Keeping the law means heeding God's teaching. Gluttons represent companions ruled by excess.
units.summary: A discerning son keeps instruction, while company given to excess can bring family shame.
units.principle: The company we keep can reveal and shape our response to instruction.
units.insight: A learner can choose close companions without treating others with contempt.
units.application: Choose companions whose habits support the commitments you want to keep.

rel.note: The sinner's wealth is likewise pictured passing out of his hands.

units.notes: Usury and extortion describe gain extracted through exploitative lending.
units.summary: Exploitative gain can pass to someone who cares for the poor.
units.principle: Resources gained by exploitation offer no lasting claim to blessing.
units.insight: A vulnerable borrower deserves fair terms and practical concern.
units.application: Review one financial arrangement for terms that unfairly burden the weaker party.

rel.note: God likewise detests wicked worship and delights in upright prayer.

units.notes: Turning the ear away describes a refusal to listen to God's teaching.
units.summary: Prayer cannot substitute for a willingness to hear and obey God.
units.principle: Worship and obedience belong together.
units.insight: Recognition of disobedience can lead to honest confession and prayer.
units.application: Bring one refused instruction before God and take a step toward obedience.

rel.note: The one who digs a pit likewise falls into it.

units.notes: The pit is a trap prepared for another. Inheriting good describes the blameless person's outcome.
units.summary: The person who leads the upright astray falls into his own trap.
units.principle: Schemes against others can rebound on the schemer.
units.insight: An invitation to compromise can be refused before it gains influence.
units.application: End an effort to draw someone into a course you know is wrong.

rel.note: Self-assessed wisdom is likewise exposed as a serious obstacle to learning.

units.notes: Wise in his own eyes describes self-assurance. Searching out means seeing through the claim.
units.summary: A discerning poor person can see through a rich person's self-confidence.
units.principle: Financial success is a poor measure of judgment.
units.insight: Insight deserves a hearing even when it comes from someone with little status.
units.application: Ask for insight from someone you might otherwise overlook.

rel.note: The closing verse repeats the image of people hiding when the wicked rise.

units.notes: Glory pictures public joy. Hiding reflects fear under wicked rule.
units.summary: Righteous leadership brings public joy, while wicked rule drives people into hiding.
units.principle: Leadership shapes whether people can live and speak openly.
units.insight: People who fear retaliation may need safe ways to speak.
units.application: Create a safe way for someone affected by your decisions to raise a concern.

rel.note: Sin's cords show the need for the mercy offered here.

units.notes: Covering here means concealing one's own sins. Forsaking means turning away from them.
units.summary: God gives mercy to those who confess and forsake their sins.
units.principle: Confession and turning belong together in receiving mercy as a gift.
units.insight: Someone who has fallen can come to Christ for cleansing and seek help making a real change.
units.application: Name a wrong honestly before God and take a concrete step to leave it and repair harm.

rel.note: Repeatedly hardening oneself against correction likewise leads toward sudden ruin.

units.notes: The Hebrew says fears continually without naming the object. The NKJV conveys reverence.
units.summary: Continual reverence keeps the heart responsive, while hardness leads toward calamity.
units.principle: A teachable heart remains open to God's correction.
units.insight: A person can respond to conviction early rather than waiting for consequences.
units.application: Act on one correction you have been resisting.

rel.note: People likewise groan under wicked rule.

units.notes: A roaring lion and charging bear picture predatory danger.
units.summary: A wicked ruler over the poor is as dangerous as a charging animal.
units.principle: Authority must protect the vulnerable rather than exploit them.
units.insight: People subject to predatory authority need protection and a fair hearing.
units.application: Use your influence to challenge one practice that preys on people with little power.

rel.note: Justice establishes the land, while taking bribes undermines it.

units.notes: Covetousness includes unjust gain. Prolonged days can include durable rule.
units.summary: Greed feeds oppressive rule, while rejecting unjust gain supports stability.
units.principle: Authority is steadier when it serves people instead of private gain.
units.insight: Leaders can protect others by disclosing and refusing improper advantage.
units.application: Remove one financial incentive that could distort a decision you oversee.

rel.note: Clearing the guilty likewise corrupts justice.

units.notes: Bloodshed means grave guilt for taking a life. The pit pictures the destructive end of flight.
units.summary: Do not help someone guilty of bloodshed escape accountability.
units.principle: Helping someone evade justice can make others share in the wrong.
units.insight: Compassion and accountability can be held together.
units.application: If asked to conceal grave wrongdoing, refuse and seek an appropriate way to report it.

rel.note: Integrity gives security, while crooked conduct invites exposure.

units.notes: Blameless describes integrity. Crooked ways are contrasted with a straight walk.
units.summary: Upright conduct gives security, while crooked ways can end in a sudden fall.
units.principle: A consistent upright course avoids dangers dishonesty creates.
units.insight: Hardship alone gives no verdict on a person's integrity.
units.application: End one hidden practice that could undermine the course you are trying to keep.

rel.note: The earlier saying likewise contrasts tilling the land with chasing frivolity.

units.notes: Tilling pictures useful work. Both outcomes are described as having one's fill.
units.summary: Steady work tends to provide bread, while empty pursuits tend toward poverty.
units.principle: Effort needs a productive object.
units.insight: A person can choose useful work within their actual opportunities.
units.application: Replace time spent chasing an empty shortcut with a step in useful work.

rel.note: Diligent planning and haste likewise lead to different ends.

units.notes: Faithful describes dependable conduct. Haste puts getting rich ahead of faithfulness.
units.summary: Faithfulness brings blessing, while haste for riches brings consequences.
units.principle: Faithfulness sets limits on how wealth is pursued.
units.insight: Slow honest progress can be valued even when quick gain looks attractive.
units.application: Decline an opportunity that requires you to rush past an ethical concern.

rel.note: The sayings of the wise likewise reject partiality in judgment.

units.notes: Partiality means judging by someone's standing. A piece of bread represents a small inducement.
units.summary: Even a small benefit can tempt someone into partiality.
units.principle: Justice should hold regardless of the size of an inducement.
units.insight: An ordinary favor can be examined for the obligation it creates.
units.application: Refuse a small favor if it would compromise a fair judgment.

rel.note: Riches can quickly fly away from those who fix their attention on them.

units.notes: An evil eye describes a grasping disposition. Haste exposes what governs it.
units.summary: Greedy haste can end in the poverty it fails to foresee.
units.principle: Greed gives poor judgment about its own consequences.
units.insight: A desire for security can be examined before it becomes a pursuit of gain at any cost.
units.application: Slow down a decision driven by fear of missing a gain.

rel.note: Faithful friendship can wound honestly, while apparent affection can deceive.

units.notes: Afterward distinguishes later appreciation from the immediate effect of correction.
units.summary: Honest correction can earn more favor in time than flattery.
units.principle: Truthful help is worth more than easy praise.
units.insight: A friend can give a difficult word with patience and care.
units.application: Offer one needed correction privately and explain the good you hope it serves.

rel.note: Mistreating father or mother likewise brings shame.

units.notes: Calling the act no transgression is the excuse the proverb exposes.
units.summary: Robbing one's parents is destructive even when the offender excuses it.
units.principle: Family ties give no entitlement to another person's property.
units.insight: Family members can protect an older person's resources while treating them with dignity.
units.application: Return something taken without permission or help protect a vulnerable relative from exploitation.

rel.note: Pride produces strife, while wisdom belongs with those who receive counsel.

units.notes: Proud heart can convey a grasping appetite. Prosperity pictures fullness or well-being.
units.summary: Grasping pride stirs conflict, while trusting the LORD leads toward well-being.
units.principle: Trust in God loosens the grip of pride and greed.
units.insight: A person can pursue a fair outcome without insisting on controlling it.
units.application: In a dispute, set aside one demand rooted in self-advantage and seek a fair response.

rel.note: Wholehearted reliance on the LORD is contrasted with leaning on one's own understanding.

units.notes: Trusting one's own heart means treating one's inner judgment as sufficient.
units.summary: Trusting your own judgment alone is folly, while walking wisely leads toward deliverance.
units.principle: The heart needs guidance and guarding.
units.insight: A strong conviction can be tested without being dismissed.
units.application: Test a decision you feel sure about against Scripture and trustworthy counsel.

rel.note: The generous person is likewise blessed for sharing food with the poor.

units.notes: Hiding the eyes pictures deliberately overlooking need.
units.summary: Generosity toward the poor is blessed, while turning away brings reproach.
units.principle: Compassion acts on need rather than looking past it.
units.insight: A gift can be given freely without expecting a return.
units.application: Meet one concrete need you have noticed within your means.

rel.note: The earlier verse likewise shows people hiding when the wicked rise.

units.notes: Rising and perishing describe the fortunes of the wicked in power.
units.summary: Wicked rule drives people into hiding, while its fall gives the righteous room to flourish.
units.principle: The character of those in power shapes public life.
units.insight: People emerging from oppressive conditions may need time and support to participate openly again.
units.application: Protect a safe opportunity for people to act or speak openly.

rel.note: The troublemaker likewise faces sudden ruin without remedy.

units.notes: A hardened neck pictures resistance to being turned.
units.summary: Repeatedly refusing correction can end in sudden ruin.
units.principle: Correction is an opportunity to change course.
units.insight: A serious warning gives someone a reason to turn while there is time.
units.application: Act on a sound rebuke you have repeatedly dismissed.

rel.note: Righteous leadership likewise brings public joy, while wicked power drives people into hiding.

units.notes: Groaning pictures the burden of oppressive rule. The first line can also read when the righteous increase.
units.summary: Upright leadership brings joy, while wicked rule burdens people.
units.principle: Leadership is accountable for the burdens it places on people.
units.insight: Those under authority should have a safe way to describe its effects.
units.application: Ask someone affected by your decisions what you could do more fairly.

rel.note: The discerning son's conduct contrasts with companionship that brings shame to his father.

units.notes: Keeping company refers to repeated association. Squandering means consuming one's resources wastefully.
units.summary: Loving wisdom gladdens a father, while paying for sex squanders resources.
units.principle: What we love and whom we keep company with shape how we live.
units.insight: Someone caught in a harmful pattern can seek help changing both spending and habits.
units.application: End a pattern of spending that supports sexual wrongdoing and seek accountable help.

rel.note: Righteousness likewise establishes a throne.

units.notes: Establishes means makes firm. Bribes buy favorable treatment.
units.summary: Justice establishes a land, while bribery undermines it.
units.principle: Corruption at the top damages the people it should serve.
units.insight: People can help protect public trust by refusing benefits that distort judgment.
units.application: Disclose and refuse any benefit that would compromise a decision you oversee.

rel.note: Honest correction can win greater favor in time than flattery.

units.notes: A concealed net pictures the trap hidden by flattering speech.
units.summary: Flattery can lay a trap for a neighbor.
units.principle: Praise deserves scrutiny when it is used to obtain something.
units.insight: An unexpected compliment can be received without giving immediate agreement to the request that follows.
units.application: Ask what an appealing request actually requires before agreeing to it.

rel.note: The sinner is likewise caught in the cords of his own wrongdoing.

units.notes: A snare is a hidden trap. Singing pictures freedom and gladness.
units.summary: Sin can trap the person who practices it, while the righteous can rejoice.
units.principle: A chosen course can produce bondage or freedom.
units.insight: A person caught in wrongdoing can begin by naming how it has bound them.
units.application: Identify one trap your own conduct has created and take a step toward leaving it.

rel.note: The poor are protected against oppression at the gate, and the LORD pleads their cause.

units.notes: Cause refers to a claim or plea for justice.
units.summary: The righteous attend to the rights of the poor.
units.principle: Justice begins by taking vulnerable people's claims seriously.
units.insight: A person with little influence may need help getting their case heard.
units.application: Listen carefully to a claim from someone with little leverage and help them seek a fair hearing.

rel.note: Hot temper stirs strife, while patience helps quiet contention.

units.notes: Setting a city aflame pictures fanning public conflict.
units.summary: Scoffers inflame a city, while the wise help calm its anger.
units.principle: How we speak can affect the peace of a whole community.
units.insight: A measured voice can reduce pressure in a public disagreement.
units.application: Decline to amplify a mocking report and offer a calm, truthful account instead.

rel.note: Answering folly on its own terms risks being drawn into the same conduct.

units.notes: Contending may include arguing a case. The second line gives rage and laughter as alternatives.
units.summary: A dispute with a fool can remain unsettled whether the response is rage or ridicule.
units.principle: Discussion requires willingness to address the matter honestly.
units.insight: Someone can pause a conversation that has stopped engaging the issue.
units.application: End an unproductive exchange and return only when the issue can be discussed on its merits.

rel.note: The wise are also told to rescue people being drawn toward death.

units.notes: Bloodthirsty describes people prepared for violence. The second line literally speaks of seeking a life and has another reading.
units.summary: The violent hate the blameless, while the upright seek to protect them.
units.principle: Integrity calls for protecting people threatened by violence.
units.insight: Someone targeted for acting uprightly may need active support.
units.application: Take a safe, concrete step to help protect someone facing a threat.

rel.note: Knowledge spares words, and understanding keeps a steady temper.

units.notes: Venting all describes releasing feelings without restraint.
units.summary: Wisdom governs the expression of feelings rather than venting them all at once.
units.principle: Restraint can make honest expression more constructive.
units.insight: Strong feelings can be acknowledged and discussed without directing them at others unchecked.
units.application: Pause before venting and choose a fitting time to describe what you actually feel.

rel.note: A just king values people who tell him the truth.

units.notes: Servants here include the officials who work under the ruler.
units.summary: A ruler who welcomes lies encourages corruption among his officials.
units.principle: Authority shapes which habits others learn to practice.
units.insight: People can be more candid when leaders make truthful disagreement safe.
units.application: Ask for evidence and invite truthful disagreement before acting on a favorable report.

rel.note: The LORD made the rich and the poor alike.

units.notes: Giving light to the eyes pictures God giving sight and life.
units.summary: The LORD gives life and sight to the poor person and the oppressor alike.
units.principle: A shared dependence on God makes the abuse of power accountable to Him.
units.insight: People can uphold equal dignity while confronting a real imbalance of power.
